q-8008:
To find the points where the hyperbola intersects the line $y=1,$ we substitute $y=1$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{6}-\frac{(1)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{6}-\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{6} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the hyperbola intersects the horizontal line $y=1$ at the points $(\pm 3,1).$

q-8005:
To find the points where the hyperbola intersects the line $x=5,$ we substitute $x=5$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-16{y}^{2} & =144 \\ 9(5)^{2}-16{y}^{2} & =144 \\ -16{y}^{2} & =144-225 \\ -16{y}^{2} & =-81 \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{81}{16} \\ y & =\pm \frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the hyperbola intersects the vertical line $x=5$ at the points $(5,\pm \frac{9}{4}).$

q-71982:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{(2\sqrt{3})}^{2}} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the second quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{2})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3})| \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=4$ and $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{3}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get 

$$
z=4\,{\text{e}}^{2\pi \text{i}/3}.
$$

q-8077:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =2\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-2}{2})| \\  & =2\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)| \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=2\sqrt{2}$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{4}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=2\sqrt{2}\,{\text{e}}^{7\pi \text{i}/4}.
$$

q-71974:
The complex number shown in the Argand diagram can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x+\text{i}y \\  & =-4-4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

To write it in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the third quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi +|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi +|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-4}{-4})| \\  & =\pi +|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)| \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=4\sqrt{2}$ and $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{4}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get 

$$
z=4\sqrt{2}\,{\text{e}}^{5\pi \text{i}/4}.
$$

q-17513:
The complex number shown in the Argand diagram can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x+\text{i}y \\  & =3+2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

To write it in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the first quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2}{3}) \\  & ≈0.588.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=\sqrt{13}$ and $\theta =0.588$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get 

$$
z=\sqrt{13}\,{\text{e}}^{0.588\,\text{i}}.
$$

q-40790:

q-120156:
Notice that the given curve is a circle of radius $\frac{2}{3}$ centered at the origin.

Therefore, its polar equation is $r=\frac{2}{3}.$

q-120182:
A circle of radius $k$ centered at the origin has the polar equation $r=k.$

We can compute the radius $k$ of our circle using the Pythagorean theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}k & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{17}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the circle is $r=\sqrt{17}.$

q-84699:
The area scale factor of a linear transformation $T$ with standard matrix $T$ is equal to $|det(T)|.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|det(T)| & =|6\cdot 8-7\cdot 4| \\  & =|48-28| \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

q-164170:
Recall that for any linear transformation $T,$ we have the following connection between the area of $D$ and the area of the image $T(D)$ under the action of $T:$

$$
\text{Area}(T(D))=|det(T)|\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

From the diagram, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {3}^{2}=9\pi .
$$

Computing the determinant of $T,$ we get 

$$
det(T)=4\cdot (-2)-(-3)\cdot 2=-2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(D)) & =|det(T)|\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =|-2|\cdot 9\pi  \\  & =18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

q-80131:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=4 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=1\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={4}^{2}+{1}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =16+1 \\ {R}^{2} & =17 \\ R & =\sqrt{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

q-80126:
The sum formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\sqrt{7} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=3\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(\sqrt{7})^{2}+{3}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =7+9 \\ {R}^{2} & =16 \\ R & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

q-11295:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=3 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=2\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(2)^{2}+(3)^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =4+9 \\ {R}^{2} & =13 \\ R & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

q-124143:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v \\ u+3v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v \\ u+3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the image of $P$ under the action of $T,$ we first create a column vector $u$ containing the coordinates of $P:$

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Applying $T$ to $u,$ we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of ${P}^{′}$ are $(6,-5).$
